items.title: Alex Karp put Palantir’s early sales team in the Mandarin Oriental instead of a Motel 6—at 10x the price
items.summary:
The old advice to dress for the job you want can apply to lodging, too—at least in the thinking of some enterprising executives. In its early days, Palantir Technologies put its young staffers up at a luxury Mandarin Oriental for sales trips instead of booking a budget chain like Motel 6.

The call came from Alex Karp, Palantir’s cofounder and CEO, and the logic was simple: In enterprise sales, appearances can matter as much as the bottom line. Even companies that will someday be worth hundreds of billions often start out with a “fake it ’til you make it” mentality.

Garry Tan, who was Palantir’s 10th employee and is now CEO of startup accelerator Y Combinator, shared the story in a May 2025 post on X :

“Funny early Palantir story.

We were doing some of our first sales meetings for Palantir and (team was all under 25 at the time) and were staying at the Mandarin Oriental.

We said hey this is a startup! Why are we wasting money on this?

Alex Karp said the people you’re selling to will ask you where you are staying. And we aren’t selling Motel 6 software. We are selling Mandarin Oriental software.”

From long shot to a $386 billion company 

Karp’s bet on looking the part has aged well. Palantir began trading on the New York Stock Exchange through a direct listing in September 2020 and was valued at about $18 billion after its first trades. As of Nov. 16, 2026, it was worth about $386 billion, per CompaniesMarketCap .

That valuation is disproportionate to its sales. As Fortune has reported, Palantir became one of the world’s 25 most valuable companies while still too…
items.t: Alex Karp put Palantir’s early sales team in the Mandarin Oriental instead of a Motel 6—at 10x the price

items.title: How much will Anthropic be worth at IPO? New platforms like Polymarket offer early clues
items.summary:
Anthropic doesn’t start trading on Nasdaq until Thursday, but prediction markets are already taking bets on what the Claude maker will be worth at the end of its debut. A Polymarket contract tied to Anthropic’s closing market capitalization has drawn nearly $10 million in trading volume. The leading bet, with odds of around 43%, is that Anthropic finishes the day worth between $1.25 trillion and $1.5 trillion. A finish below $1.25 trillion isn’t far behind at roughly 35%, while the odds of topping $1.5 trillion are about 20%.

On Hyperliquid, a crypto exchange specializing in perpetual futures , one contract put Anthropic’s implied valuation at roughly $1.7 trillion, according to CoinGecko data . The contract trades around the clock, letting traders bet on what the company is worth without buying a single share.

The estimates come as Anthropic prepares to set the price for its initial public offering Wednesday and begin trading on Nasdaq a day later under the ticker symbol ANT. The Claude maker initially sought $70 to $78 a share. At $78, the offering would total about $64 billion and value the company at roughly $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis, but strong demand could push the IPO price higher.

Platforms with roots in crypto offer an early read on what traders expect.

Over the past two years, Kalshi and Polymarket have become go-to places to bet on everything from sports and politics to pop culture. Contracts tied to how a stock performs or where it closes have also gained traction and are now a regular feature on both platforms.

Hyperliquid gained a following…
items.t: How much will Anthropic be worth at IPO? New platforms like Polymarket offer early clues

items.title: After a week of outages that put IT resiliency to the test, CIOs are already preparing for the next disruption
items.summary:
It all started on Thursday when a Microsoft outage disrupted workplace services including Outlook, Teams, and Copilot. One day later, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop that halted departures across the nation, upending travel plans for more than 1.5 million passengers. 

Even more disruptions have cascaded throughout this week: yet another outage affected banking websites and apps run by financial giants including Wells Fargo and Capital One , then at United Airlines , Apple , and a downed internal communications network at the National Security Agency.

There is no evidence that these systems disruptions affecting banking, airlines, tech giants, and the government are connected. But the heightened attention on disruptions that have affected major technology systems that most take for granted puts more attention on the reliability and resiliency of IT; how to communicate the latest developments of an outage to employees, customers, executives, and the board; and already has begun the process to develop post-mortem reports to assess how a system disruption was handled and what parts of their business continuity plans could be improved.

“Our approach is that resilience doesn’t really come from a document or a backup system,” says Jordan Ruch, chief information and digital officer at New Jersey-based health system AtlantiCare. “It is a muscle organizations build and it comes from planning with operations before something happens.”

Across corporate America, the biggest disruption to business operations this past week was the outage at Microsoft, which…

items.title: Skilled trades leaders admit ‘nothing is future-proof’—but AI can’t replace America’s growing demand for blue-collar workers like auto technicians
items.summary:
As AI forces office workers to rethink how tasks get done, skilled trades jobs have largely been seen as a more insulated, safer path to a six-figure career . However, hands-on roles like plumbers, electricians , and auto technicians aren’t exactly immune to the changes sweeping the workforce, either.

“Nothing is future-proof,” Mary Culler, president of Ford Philanthropy, said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Summit on Tuesday. “But I do think that a lot of the skilled trades are just those jobs that are going to be required to have a human there.”

Auto technicians—who are in short supply , for example —could increasingly use AI to help diagnose vehicle problems, she said, but still need a human to do the actual manual labor. 

Carhartt CEO Linda Hubbard echoed that AI-powered efficiency will change how skilled trades workers do their jobs—but she said that the industry’s labor needs—fueled by the data center boom and broader infrastructure investments—will continue to outpace any productivity gains from the technology.

“No matter how good we get at encouraging people, I think we’re always going to be challenged to get the number of people that we need into the trades to just rebuild the infrastructure of the country,” Hubbard said on stage in an interview with Fortune ’s Kristin Stoller.

Employers are expected to fill approximately 1.7 million skilled trades openings annually between now and 2034—but roughly a quarter of the industry’s existing 18 million workers are over 55 and nearing retirement .

Six-figure salaries and business ownership are within reach for Gen…
items.t: Skilled trades leaders admit ‘nothing is future-proof’—but AI can’t replace America’s growing demand for blue-collar workers like auto technicians

items.title: Mississippi gov. says AI infrastructure messaging went sour when it stopped being about necessity: ‘Everybody in America uses data centers regularly’
items.summary:
U.S. voters made their opinions on data centers known at the ballot box this month—opposing data center expansion in 52 of 53 measures in the midterm elections—but Republican Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves believes Americans have lost track of the necessity of the AI infrastructure buildout.

Speaking with Fortune Executive Editor Lee Clifford at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Tuesday, Reeves argued many Americans don’t realize how often they rely on AI infrastructure in their day-to-day lives. He said when he meets with large groups in his state and across the U.S., he tells them to pick up and look at their cell phone, asking if they’ve used the device today, particularly their GPS.

“And if the answer is yes, then you have used a data center today, and everybody in America uses data centers regularly,” Reeves said. “And so, in terms of necessity and the need for everyday American citizens, it is without question that there is going to be a need to keep this data.” 

Mississippi has 38 data center projects total , including 17 operational data centers. Earlier this year, Amazon announced a $25 billion investment in data centers in the state. However, research has overwhelmingly shown Americans oppose local data center construction on the grounds of environmental concerns, as well as fears of climbing utilities bills and electricity costs. 

Reeves argued data centers’ utility goes beyond technology in his constituents’ pockets, and that they are an asset to national security. He cited litigation between the NAACP and xAI, in which the NAACP Mississippi…
items.t: Mississippi gov. says AI infrastructure messaging went sour when it stopped being about necessity: ‘Everybody in America uses data centers regularly’

items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...
items.t: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes

items.title: Trump said colleges would ‘go to hell very quickly’ without foreign students. New enrollment just fell 18%, costing them billions in tuition
items.summary:
New international students at U.S. colleges fell 18% in the 2025–26 school year, to 228,123, the Institute of International Education said Monday in its annual Open Doors report . The first look at this fall points to a second straight drop. In IIE’s fall 2026 snapshot of more than 800 schools, new international enrollment fell another 15%.

The total looks calmer: 1,146,163 international students, down 3%. But that count includes 335,785 graduates on Optional Practical Training, the program that lets them work in the U.S. after their degree. That group rose 14%, and it pays no tuition. Take it out and the number of international students enrolled in classes fell about 8%, a figure IIE confirmed to Fortune. That’s about 73,000 fewer students paying tuition.

The president saw this coming. At a cabinet meeting in August 2025 , defending a plan to admit 600,000 Chinese students, Trump said that without them, “our college system would go to hell very quickly and it wouldn’t be the top colleges. It would be colleges that struggle on the bottom.” His base pushed back. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene said that if keeping Chinese students out made some schools fail, “these schools should fail anyways because they are being propped up by the CCP.”

Since then, his administration has moved the other way. In May 2025 the State Department paused student visa interviews, then restarted them with expanded social media vetting. A travel ban that started with 19 countries grew to 39, plus the Palestinian territory, on Jan. 1. In July, DHS finalized a rule replacing open-ended student status…
items.t: Trump said colleges would ‘go to hell very quickly’ without foreign students. New enrollment just fell 18%, costing them billions in tuition

items.title: ‘The Romans are laughing at us’: physical AI founder raises $97 million in quest to stop wasting time with archaic infrastructure maintenance
items.summary:
Alex Hawkinson keeps a collection of Roman artifacts at BrightAI’s robot demo center, and he has a saying to go with them: “The Romans are laughing at us.”

Think of the way the Romans inspected their roads, Hawkinson told Fortune : “They sent teams of technicians out periodically on schedule” to check on their infrastructure. Two thousand years later, power companies, water utilities, and pipeline operators still do. In his telling, two out of three of those trips turn up nothing to fix, and the failures that matter happen in between visits anyway.

Hawkinson is convinced this can change, and investors are paying for the idea. BrightAI said Wednesday it has raised $97 million in a round led by Smith Point Capital , the growth-stage firm started by former Salesforce co-CEO Keith Block. GE Vernova, already a BrightAI customer, also invested, along with Cobalt Capital, Marlinspike Partners, Zero Infinity Partners as well as existing backers Khosla Ventures, Inspired Capital, and Upfront Ventures. The round brings total funding to $184 million and values BrightAI at $750 million, according to a person familiar with the matter. Hawkinson insisted he “doesn’t care” about so-called unicorn status: The point is bring infrastructure out of the ancient Roman era.

His pitch has three parts. Replace scheduled human inspections with sensors and AI that watch infrastructure all the time. Go after what BrightAI estimates is more than $7 trillion a year in waste worldwide. And along the way, create a kind of data that has never existed: a continuous record of how pipes, poles, and pumps…
items.t: ‘The Romans are laughing at us’: physical AI founder raises $97 million in quest to stop wasting time with archaic infrastructure maintenance

items.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
items.summary:
After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs

When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI.

But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

items.title: ‘If you don’t act now, it will be existential’: Defense tech CEOs say Pentagon’s ‘Industrial Age’ bureaucracy must adapt
items.summary:
As AI-enabled drones transform the way wars are fought in Ukraine and Iran, two leaders of military tech startups warned on Tuesday that the Pentagon has to move faster to keep up with modern warfare. 

“There’s a growing realization that if you don’t act now, it will be existential in the near future,” Tyler Sweatt, CEO of defense software deployment company Second Front Systems, told Fortune ’s Allie Garfinkle at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum .

While venture money is pouring into defense tech at record levels, the Pentagon hasn’t sped up to match, and investors want returns. Sweatt said that pressure means defense tech companies will likely consolidate in “a tranche of deals” in the next six months. Shield AI, the autonomous weapon developer whose CEO Gary Steele joined Sweatt onstage, has already started: It announced Nov. 5 that it’s raising $2.5 billion to support its acquisition of radar systems company Echodyne in a transaction valued at $5.3 billion.

Sweatt and Steele said the Pentagon’s lengthy approval processes and outdated systems could keep new tech from reaching troops quickly enough. Sweatt described the Pentagon as an “Industrial Age organization” bogged down with “big long bureaucracies” and “antiquated technology production lines” that will have to change. 

“We’re at the beginning of this journey, not the end of this journey,” Steele added. “It will take time because things move slowly; the technology is not moving slowly.”

Sweatt and Steele’s concerns echo those of a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report published in July, which found the…
items.t: ‘If you don’t act now, it will be existential’: Defense tech CEOs say Pentagon’s ‘Industrial Age’ bureaucracy must adapt

President, who had agreed to sit for deposition in October but backed out, must now appear by 22 January

Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge, gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned.

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
items.summary:
Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

items.title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
items.summary:
Stock market debut of Claude AI chatbot maker is expected to be one of the biggest flotations in history

The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history.

The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed.
